newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. chief calls for binding treaty on terrorism.
newsitem.headline: U.N. chief calls for binding treaty on terrorism.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali on Thursday called for a new binding treaty to combat international terrorism and said it was high time for states to cooperate with each other.

While at least 11 treaties or conventions against terrorism were in force, they were piecemeal and had little monitoring machinery, he said in a prepared speech to Harvard's Kennedy School of Government in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

"My call today for a general international anti-terrorist instrument is, therefore, a call for a comprehensive legal framework for the fight against international terrorism in all its aspects," he said.
Boutros-Ghali also acknowledged threats against him and spoke of the murders of his prime minister grandfather and Egyptian President Anwar Sadat.
"Terrorism has touched my life," he said.
"I was with President Anwar Sadat on his historic trip to Jerusalem, to Camp David and at the signing of the Treaty of Peace between Egypt and Israel," he said.
"For these achievements, President Sadat was assassinated by terrorists and I have to live with this threat."
Boutros-Ghali's grandfather, Prime Minister Boutros Pasha Ghali, was gunned down in 1910 by a radical Moslem for his supposed closeness to British colonialists.

Sadat, murdered in 1981, had appointed Boutros-Ghali, as deputy foreign minister and made him a key negotiator at the Camp David talks that resulted in the 1979 peace treaty. For this he was castigated in the Arab world for many years as "the academic engineer of Arab surrender."

Despite many calls for international action against terrorism, Boutros-Ghali said some difficulties had to be taken into consideration, such as states making arrangements with terrorists in exchange for being left alone.

"Some governments resist or hesitate to cooperate against international terrorism due to national security," he said. "Fearing that they themselves will be targeted, they make quiet or tacit arrangements to leave terrorists alone in return for being left alone."

Others, he said, deprive innocent people of civil rights under cover of a claimed necessity to take anti-terrorist precautions." And some states were hesitant in sharing intelligence of grounds of national security.
At present 11 treaties addressing crimes associated with terrorism have been deposited with the United Nations, including terrorism against diplomats, aircraft, navigation and nuclear materials.

But Boutros-Ghali said a much more comprehensive legal framework was needed to include bombings, fund-raising, arms traffic, the use of weapons of mass destruction and an exchange of information on suspects.
"Unilateral and even bilateral action is not sufficient to deal with a threat that is global," he said.
